transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-06-14 08:30 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Recording: remote (auto-transcript)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE), Aria Singh (BorealGrid CTO), Noah Patel (Lead ML Eng), Sofia Martinez (Platform Eng)

Summary: brief discovery focused on p95 latency targets, concurrent token fan-out behavior during webhooks and streaming, and fallback strategies (quantized models, regional fallbacks). Customer leaning toward starting hosted pilot but wants private/VPC eval for compliance.

Topics covered:
- Target p95 SLA: 200–350 ms for short-chat (<=64 tokens), 800–1200 ms for streaming longer responses (p95)
- Expected concurrency and burst profile: steady 200 RPS, burst to 3k concurrent streams for 10–20s, token/sec load during burst up to 450k tokens/sec
- Fallback options: smaller quantized variants, cross-region routing, Dedicated reserved pool with burst capacity
- Security: KMS, SSO/SAML, audit logs and data residency
- Benchmarks: request for token/sec scripts, KV cache warm/cold behavior, cold-start times

Action items (short list in call):
- Redwood to send pricing and bench runbook
- Customer to provide traffic CSV and sample prompts
- Schedule follow-up pilot planning session

Questions raised:
- How does Dedicated handle KV cache across scaled pods?
- What's typical p95 degradation when KV cache cold or after autoscale events?
- Can we stream partial tokens to mobile clients while preserving context and SLO?

Transcript: (timestamps approximate, transcription has noise and occasional mislabels)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro — I'm Maya, your AE, and Liam will go deep on the performance bits.
[00:12] Aria Singh: Hi Maya, hi Liam. thanks, we're excited, we've been trying to size this for our new chat assistant. big concern is p95 while people are on web chat and mobile streaming.
[00:23] Liam Ortiz: Great. Can you share the numbers you're aiming for? p95 and concurrency?
[00:28] Noah Patel: Yeah so for basic customer support flows we want p95 under 300ms for responses under 64 tokens. For longer documents / summarizations, p95 up to 1.2s is okay. But the hard part is token fan-out when every client streams — we can suddenly see 2,500 to 3,000 concurrent open streams.
[00:45] Sofia Martinez: And those bursts last about 10–30 seconds, like after a marketing email or outage. steady state is more like 150–250 qps.
[00:53] Liam Ortiz: That's helpful. So two things to think about: steady-state capacity vs burst. Redwood Dedicated gives you reserved pool and we support burst overcommit you can configure, but for Hosted we have autoscaling with smart routing and fallbacks.
[01:07] Aria Singh: Can you explain fallback? like if a zone gets saturated, do you route to smaller model? or drop connections?
[01:14] Liam Ortiz: The usual is multi-tier fallback: first route to a compatible lower-capacity variant — often a quantized 8-bit variant — which reduces token/sec cost and latency. second, cross-region fallback if latency budget allows. third, degrade streaming to chunked partial tokens or lower sampling settings. there is also an option to queue short requests for up to X ms.
[01:39] Noah Patel: What's the p95 hit when you go to the quantized variant? we worry about quality regressions.
[01:45] Liam Ortiz: Usually model-specific. for many decoder-only models we see a 5–15% change in latency p95 (improvement) but quality varies; Redwood Optimize can suggest which workloads tolerate quantized variants and where to pin baseline for canary. apologies, I said Redwood Optima earlier in a doc — but it's Redwood Optimize.
[02:03] Aria Singh: And for streaming — we need token/sec and partial streaming latency. do you have numbers for token/sec per GPU with KV cache warm?
[02:12] Liam Ortiz: ballpark: on modern A100/RTX-class instances with well-optimized kernels, a single GPU can sustain ~50–120k tokens/sec depending on model size and sequence length distribution. with continuous batching and warm KV cache, streaming p95 for short tokens can be under 200–300ms.
[02:32] Noah Patel: That seems optimistic — our internal tests on a 4xV100 setup peaked at 70k tokens/sec but degraded quickly under cold KV.
[02:40] Liam Ortiz: Cold KV is tough — if the KV cache is cold you'll see a larger p95 tail for the initial tokens while caches fill, our runtime pre-warms hot prefixes for common prompts to mitigate. part of the pilot is to run a warm-up phase.
[02:56] Sofia Martinez: For VPC/private deployment, how does the control plane talk to the runtime, and can we keep all tensors/weights in our network?
[03:05] Liam Ortiz: For Private we deliver a customer-managed control plane with the runtime in your VPC or on-prem. Keys can stay in your KMS/HSM. We also provide audit logs and RBAC and you can disable outbound telemetry if needed. I should flag that SOC two evidence and ISO documents are available — folks sometimes call those S O C two in notes.
[03:22] Aria Singh: Good. Also we have strict data residency for some enterprise customers — EU-only. Does Redwood support region pinning?
[03:29] Maya Chen: Yes, you can pin model serving to specific regions for Private and Dedicated. For Hosted accounts we have region-level controls and can route only to GDPR-compliant regions.
[03:38] Noah Patel: back to benchmarking: can you share a runbook? we want to reproduce p95 numbers locally before the pilot so we can compare apples-to-apples.
[03:45] Liam Ortiz: Absolutely. We'll share a benchmark runbook: synthetic load scripts for token/sec and streaming, guidelines for KV warm/cold phases, and a sample client for mobile streaming. we typically recommend a 3-phased test: cold-start bench, warm steady-state, and burst stress tests.
[04:01] Aria Singh: For burst, our biggest worry is lots of simultaneous streams that each request 200–400 tokens. network egress and token accounting matter for cost. can Dedicated give us predictable cost during bursts?
[04:11] Maya Chen: Dedicated is contracted capacity — you reserve GPUs and get predictable throughput. we also have burst capacity add-ons so short spikes can use extra pooled capacity at a predefined marginal rate. that helps with predictable economics vs pure usage-billing in Hosted.
[04:27] Noah Patel: what's the minimum commit?
[04:29] Maya Chen: We have monthly and annual commitments; minimum depends on region and GPU type — I'll include a grid in the pricing doc.
[04:36] Sofia Martinez: On the technical side, how does autoscale affect p95? if you're ramping up new pods do you rehydrate KV caches?
[04:44] Liam Ortiz: Yes autoscale events cause cold caches on newly provisioned nodes. Redwood's runtime minimizes cold-cache pain via prefix replication and fast KV sync for hot keys. in highly bursty workloads we advise a hybrid pattern: a small baseline Dedicated pool to keep hot prefixes warm + Hosted autoscale for extra capacity.
[05:02] Aria Singh: That hybrid idea is interesting. Can you show a sizing example? say we want p95 <= 300ms for short chat, steady 200 QPS, bursts to 3k concurrent streams with avg 150 tokens per stream.
[05:16] Liam Ortiz: rough calc: steady-state token rate: 200 qps * 50 tokens avg = 10k tokens/sec. burst: 3k streams * 150 tokens over 20s ~ (3k*150)/20 = 22.5k tokens/sec during the burst — actually that math looks low; if streams are concurrent and streaming tokens/sec per stream is ~3–5 tokens/sec, you can reach 9–15k tokens/sec. if they all request full responses instantly you hit token peaks. worth getting your 48-hour traffic CSV we asked for to model shapes precisely.
[05:54] Noah Patel: sorry, our ops estimate said bursts produce up to 450k tokens/sec for a peak 10s window because of fan-out from webhooks — each incoming event fan-outs to 120 downstream user streams.
[06:05] Liam Ortiz: Ah okay that's a different pattern — event-driven fan-out multiplies tokens heavily. for that you want a combination of edge buffering + batching and potentially an async workflow: respond with a short immediate reply and queue longer outputs to background workers served by Dedicated pools. we can also route fan-out traffic to cheaper quantized instances for background generation.
[06:26] Aria Singh: Do you have a reference architecture for fan-out?
[06:29] Liam Ortiz: Yes, we'll attach a diagram. high-level: edge gateway -> rate limiter/queue -> initial short response (streamed) -> background generation service writing back to user channels. key is to avoid synchronous heavy generation on the hot path.
[06:45] Sofia Martinez: Regarding observability, we need token-level cost breakdown by route and by token type, and per-route p95 dashboards. is that in Redwood Console?
[06:54] Maya Chen: Redwood Console provides per-route/model token counts, p95 latency, token cost, and trace-level drilldowns. retention tiers are configurable under add-ons.
[07:06] Aria Singh: our security team will want to see audit logs, KMS integrations, and SOC 2/ISO attestation. can you share docs?
[07:13] Maya Chen: yes we'll send security packet (SOC2, ISO, pen test summary), architecture diagram for private deployment, and KMS integration guide.
[07:21] Noah Patel: on eval timeline — we want to run a 4-week pilot with throughput and streaming SLAs. can Redwood do that?
[07:28] Maya Chen: Yes we run pilots. Typical pilot includes: baseline sizing, shared test harness, joint benchmark run, and production-like traffic replay. we often do canary rollouts and a two-week validation window.
[07:39] Liam Ortiz: for the pilot, we'll instrument KV cold/warm measurements, measure p95 across 50th/95th/99th, and generate a regression report if we swap quantized models.
[07:50] Aria Singh: on cost, are there levers to reduce unit token cost without sacrificing p95?
[07:56] Liam Ortiz: Yes — batching, persistent KV caching, prefix caching, and model quantization. Redwood Optimize will analyze prompt sets and recommend batching thresholds and which model variants to use for different routes. occasionally reducing sampling temperature or truncating to shorter context helps too.
[08:12] Sofia Martinez: we run sensitive PII — are there options for zero-retention or customer-controlled retention?
[08:17] Maya Chen: Yes. Private deployments allow full control. Hosted can be configured with short retention and no training usage, plus we support customer-managed encryption keys.
[08:25] Aria Singh: quick nit — how is streaming priced? per token inbound/outbound? some vendors bill per stream minute.
[08:30] Maya Chen: We bill per token for both generation and embedding units; streaming doesn't add a separate stream-minute charge. you can see per-route token economics in the Console.
[08:38] Noah Patel: if we hand off long responses to background workers on Dedicated, does that change how tokens are billed?
[08:44] Maya Chen: Billed per token regardless of sync/async — but Dedicated has committed capacity pricing so your marginal unit economics differ vs Hosted usage billing. we'll include example tables.
[08:54] Aria Singh: Any caveats about quantized models and hallucination rates? we can't accept big regressions.
[08:59] Liam Ortiz: it's model- and prompt-dependent. that's why we run canary tests with your prompts. Redwood Optimize flags prompts that regress beyond a threshold and suggests alternatives or locks those routes to full-precision variants.
[09:12] Sofia Martinez: for SLA language, what's typical p95 SLO in contracts?
[09:16] Maya Chen: For Dedicated enterprise contracts we can commit to per-route p95 SLOs with credits for missed targets; for Hosted we publish performance profiles and can offer SLAs for enterprise tiers. we'll include sample SLA language.
[09:29] Aria Singh: one last technical: what's cold-start time for large models in Private on bare-metal?
[09:35] Liam Ortiz: booting weights and JIT warmup are the heavy parts — typical cold-start to first token for a big model can be tens of seconds without pre-warm; with pinned Dedicated or warm-standby it's sub-second for subsequent requests.
[09:49] Maya Chen: ok this has been super helpful. recap quick: we'll send pricing + pilot contract, Liam will send benchmark runbook and scripts, and Noah will upload traffic CSV and prompts. schedule follow-up workshop week of 6/24.
[10:05] Aria Singh: sounds good. also please include the diagram for fan-out architecture, and any notes about KV pre-warm strategies.
[10:12] Liam Ortiz: will do. I'll also include sample results from a fan-out stress test we ran that shows token/sec during a 15s spike and how latencies behaved under warm vs cold KV. note: some of the sample numbers in the doc were on older infra so we will label the GPU types.
[10:29] (brief off-topic: small talk about weather and a conference)
[12:10] Maya Chen: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with next steps.
[12:15] Aria Singh: thanks.

End of transcript.
